strengths: Addresses a relevant accountability problem with a clear registration, watermarking, detection, and attribution pipeline. The distinction between detection and correct user attribution is useful.

Reports strong clean-image results across three generators with 100,000 user watermarks, plus a million-user experiment. Threshold, watermark-length, corruption, and worst-user analyses provide useful empirical coverage.

A-BSTA improves watermark separation and worst-user attribution over Random and NRG in the reported experiments, with an average assignment time of 24 ms. The paper supplies pseudocode and explicitly acknowledges inherited white-box vulnerabilities.
weaknesses: Theorem 3 has a substantive correctness problem: Appendix D factorizes match-event probabilities without establishing independence. Independent watermark selection does not generally make scores against the same decoded string independent. For uniform two-bit decoder output, threshold 0.75, and independently sampled watermarks from {00,01} and {10,11}, actual FDR is 0.5, exceeding the claimed bound of 0.4375. Section 6.6 additionally applies this theorem to A-BSTA watermarks, whose selection is explicitly dependent.

The theoretical guarantees rely on independent decoded bits and, for watermarked content, identical per-bit accuracy. These assumptions are not empirically validated. Estimating parameters on the test data and comparing aggregate results in two settings does not establish their applicability. Section 5.5 also incorrectly infers that actual detection and attribution rates are close because their lower bounds are close.

Novelty and comparisons are insufficiently established. Assigning user fingerprints and applying minimum-distance decoding closely connects to classical fingerprinting and error-correcting codes, which receive inadequate treatment. A-BSTA modifies an existing algorithm through depth truncation and random initialization, without an approximation guarantee. Comparisons omit structured codebooks and computation-matched randomized search.

The false-detection evaluation uses only 1,000 negative images. Even observing zero errors gives a one-sided 95% upper confidence bound of approximately 0.003, leaving rare false accusations poorly characterized. Large numbers of watermark assignments also reuse only 1,000 source test images per generator. Missing confidence intervals and repeated runs weaken conclusions about worst-user performance and algorithmic improvements.

Robustness evidence is limited to one image watermarking backbone at 128×128 resolution, four corruption families included during training, and one black-box attack. Attribution-specific collusion and framing are not evaluated. Reported SSIM measures post-processing damage relative to watermarked images, leaving the quality cost of watermark insertion unquantified.

The text experiment watermarks WikiText-2 passages rather than actual language-model outputs. Length-constrained paraphrasing and the absence of text-quality measurements further limit its support for the claimed applicability to AI-generated text.
